extracted.intended_audience: gentlemen and general readers of early-18th-century London (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive observations and practical advice about male behaviour, honour, courage, ageing, and how to comport oneself to succeed with women and in society. The essay contrasts virtue and pleasure, mechanical versus heroic courage, and catalogs traits that make a 'woman's man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of pursuing Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who make delight the chief purpose of life give up the delicacy of their passions to appetites, pursue disappointing gratifications, and lose higher joys; pleasure approaches with warm wishes and gay looks but leaves disorder, impotence, shame, and conscious imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and consequences: 'She makes our Youth inglorious, our Age shameful.' The writer cites Will. Honeycomb's boasts and general caricature of a life spent in jollity to illustrate the hollowness and long-term harm of such pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man of Wit and Pleasure is negligent in duties
rubrics_metrics.description: A man whose chief character is wit and pleasure is a negligent friend, father, and husband, and entails poverty on his descendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences enumerated: mortgages, diseases, and settlements are the usual legacies such men leave; many who end in Tyburn had earlier been 'Men of Wit and Pleasure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Irresolution and procrastination flow from pleasure addiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Addiction to pleasure produces irresolution and procrastination in all a man's affairs, bringing dishonour to gentlemen and bankruptcy to traders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay treats these as predictable moral and practical failures of a pleasure-driven life; no remedy is formalized beyond avoiding that pursuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent can mask vice (the facade of wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shining qualities of some talented people give a beauty to whatever they are engaged in, and a mixture of wit has recommended madness; thus talents have made vice tolerated or admired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary note: admiration of brilliance can excuse or conceal intemperance and moral failure; one should not let outward accomplishments justify vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of prolonged jollity on behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended engagement in jollity, mirth, wit, or humorous entertainments often leads to sharpness toward others, impertinence, ungraceful noise, unskilful openness, and calumny; in the end such people cannot recollect anything that adds to the enjoyment of their own mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete behaviours to watch for: being 'sharp to some Man he is sorry to have offended,' 'impertinent to some one it was Cruelty to treat with such Freedom,' and inability to identify lasting pleasures or honorable memories from a life of mere diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intemperate country gaiety as folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Country gentlemen who pursue intemperate meals and loud jollities destroy remaining reason: they 'drink till they cannot taste, smoak till they cannot see, and roar till they cannot hear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an anti-pattern of faux-pleasure—imitating the manners of men of wit without the genius to support such a life makes the scene 'wild to an Extravagance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical courage vs. reasoned heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: Many soldiers show a 'mechanick courage' acquired by acting always in a crowd (habit), whereas true leaders are formed by reasoning themselves into a resignation to death and a higher sense of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: mechanical courage stems from habit and the spectacle of many surviving; heroic command arises from reflection that death is natural and from pursuing duty and greater good despite personal hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a commander/heroic soldier
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanders (heroes) have reasoned resignation to dying, place duty above preservation of life, derive resolution from the impossibility of escape, value conscience of well-doing, thirst for glory, and encourage mutual love and self-sacrifice among troops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical conduct: they are foremost in danger, just in distributing rewards, modest in their own gains, beloved by officers and private men, and inspire men to risk themselves for one another rather than from fear of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: True friendship among soldiers (mutual affection)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-ordered regiment the commander is a friend and companion; private men regard each other as brethren and fear for one another's honour and safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs: mutual care in danger, officers sharing hardships, and leaders protecting men’s dignity and pay; this social bond differentiates excellent regiments from the mere mass of soldiery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly of wishing to be younger
rubrics_metrics.description: Wishing to be younger is an impertinent and irrational desire, typically expressed in view of past pleasures one cannot and should not repeat; it marks a foolish or dissolute mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive revaluation of age: reason grows stronger with years, virtuous old age provides refined pleasures (good fame, religious contemplation, respectful commerce), and memory of a well-spent youth brings unmixed pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of virtuous old age vs. sensual youth
rubrics_metrics.description: The latter part of life is more eligible for rational and worthy pleasures (conscience of good fame, contemplation of another life, respect of honest men); age enlarges capacities for such enjoyments while sensual habits of youth become burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: before age, renounce pursuits of youth so sensual habits do not haunt imagination when limbs fail; retire early into old-man habits to preserve dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty alone is a social disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: A sober, modest man is often treated as precise and unfashioned and may be disregarded in company; society rewards certain looseness of behaviour and impudence in men who wish to gain women's approbation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid being marginalized, a well-educated young man should cultivate 'a good Air at entering into a Room, a proper Audacity in expressing himself with Gaiety and Gracefulness'—small accomplishments of address and presence matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to be successful with women (the 'Woman's Man')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Woman's Man' differs in air and behaviour: loose/negligent garb, soft and indolent manner, apparent unconcern, little officious attentions (knows what's good for a cold), a bottle of spirits in pocket, knowledge of family matters, and a talent for entertaining conversation and mimicry of the woman's world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific tactics observed: singularity in behaviour that would be ridiculous among men can recommend him to women; reputation of being 'well with other women' is advantageous; impertinent quarrelling, dressing unlike others, assiduity about the fair sex, wit, humour, inconstancy, and a spiteful/dangerous tongue can all increase success. The business is to entertain—'better to have a Faculty of arguing, than a Capacity of judging right.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Society rewards showy libertinism among the fashionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Loosest principles and most abandoned behaviour often carry all before them in pretensions to women of fortune; fashion and rivalry among beauties promote acceptance of such men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: being seen as fashionable or in favour can lead other women to imitate and accept a man regardless of his true merit (the 'fashion' and rivalries among ladies create demand for such displays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immodest public discourse harms working women
rubrics_metrics.description: The unreasonable liberty men take to speak immodest things in the presence of women who must work in public (coffee-houses, shops, 'Change') is indecent and injurious to their business and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedies suggested: urge gentlemen to show deference, recognize that modest women may still keep public houses, and expose offenders (the writer suggests writing down immodest talk and publishing it). The moral: men of honour should protect vulnerable women from insult and the economic harm of impertinent gallantry.
